# Strip Out Every Copy of a Value — Explained, One Approach at a Time

<!-- Generated by scripts/gen-explained.mjs from src/data/problems/two-pointers/remove-element.ts.
     Edit the data, then run `npm run docs:explained`. Edits here are overwritten. -->

**Two Pointers** · easy · [the same question on LeetCode](https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-element/)

Given an integer array and a value, remove every occurrence of that value and hand back what survives, in the order it appeared. Do the removal inside the array you were given rather than building a second one.

## What the input promises

- 0 <= nums.length <= 100
- 0 <= nums[i] <= 50 and 0 <= val <= 100, so val may be a number that never appears at all
- the survivors keep their ORIGINAL relative order — LeetCode accepts any order, but pinning it is what lets five different implementations be compared against each other
- an empty array is legal, and so is an array where every value is val: both answer with nothing, so the code must survive a writer that never advances

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `nums = [3, 2, 2, 3], val = 3` | `[2, 2]` | — |
| `nums = [0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 0, 4, 2], val = 2` | `[0, 1, 3, 0, 4]` | The two 2s in the middle are adjacent — the writer has to fall two behind, not one. |
| `nums = [2, 2, 2], val = 2` | `[]` | Everything matches. The writer never moves, and the answer is an empty prefix. |

<details>
<summary>Hints, one nudge at a time — open them in order</summary>

1. The answer is a PREFIX: the survivors, in order, packed at the front. Nothing past that boundary matters.
2. Every position gets read, but only some get written. That is two indices moving at different speeds.
3. Where the writer stops IS the length of the answer — it never needed a separate count.

</details>

---

## 1. Delete and shift

Scan for a match and, every time one turns up, slide the whole remaining tail one slot to the left and shrink the live length.

```python
def remove_element(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        if nums[i] == val:
            for j in range(i, n - 1):
                nums[j] = nums[j + 1]
            n -= 1
        else:
            i += 1
    return nums[:n]
```

**O(n^2) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] removeElement(int[] nums, int val) {
    int n = nums.length;
    int i = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        if (nums[i] == val) {
            for (int j = i; j < n - 1; j++) nums[j] = nums[j + 1];
            n--;
        } else {
            i++;
        }
    }
    return Arrays.copyOf(nums, n);
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> removeElement(vector<int> nums, int val) {
    int n = (int)nums.size();
    int i = 0;
    while (i < n) {
        if (nums[i] == val) {
            for (int j = i; j < n - 1; j++) nums[j] = nums[j + 1];
            n--;
        } else {
            i++;
        }
    }
    nums.resize(n);
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## 2. Filter into a copy

> **Why now.** Shifting the tail on every match re-copies values that were already in the right place; an array of nothing but val does that n times, which is quadratic work to produce an empty answer. Appending the survivors somewhere else touches each value exactly once.

Collect the survivors into a fresh list in one pass and return that, leaving the original array untouched.

```python
def remove_element(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    kept = []
    for x in nums:
        if x != val:
            kept.append(x)
    return kept
```

**O(n) time · O(n) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] removeElement(int[] nums, int val) {
    int[] kept = new int[nums.length];
    int at = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x != val) {
            kept[at] = x;
            at++;
        }
    }
    return Arrays.copyOf(kept, at);
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> removeElement(vector<int> nums, int val) {
    vector<int> kept;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x != val) kept.push_back(x);
    }
    return kept;
}
```

</details>

---

## 3. Count, then compact

> **Why now.** The filtered copy is linear but it allocates a second array the size of the input just to hold values that already exist. Counting first gives the length of the answer up front, so the survivors can be packed into the array that was already there and nothing new is allocated.

One pass to count how many values survive, a second to slide them to the front of the original array, and return that many.

```python
def remove_element(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    keep = 0
    for x in nums:
        if x != val:
            keep += 1
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != val:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return nums[:keep]
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] removeElement(int[] nums, int val) {
    int keep = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x != val) keep++;
    }
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < nums.length; read++) {
        if (nums[read] != val) {
            nums[write] = nums[read];
            write++;
        }
    }
    return Arrays.copyOf(nums, keep);
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> removeElement(vector<int> nums, int val) {
    int keep = 0;
    for (int x : nums) {
        if (x != val) keep++;
    }
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < (int)nums.size(); read++) {
        if (nums[read] != val) {
            nums[write] = nums[read];
            write++;
        }
    }
    nums.resize(keep);
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## 4. Reader and writer

> **Why now.** The counting pass exists only to learn the length of the answer, and the compaction loop already knows it — the writer's index at the end is that number. Dropping the first pass halves the reads and removes a second place where the match test could be written differently by accident.

One pass with two indices: the reader visits everything, the writer only advances when a survivor is placed.

```python
def remove_element(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != val:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return nums[:write]
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] removeElement(int[] nums, int val) {
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < nums.length; read++) {
        if (nums[read] != val) {
            nums[write] = nums[read];
            write++;
        }
    }
    return Arrays.copyOf(nums, write);
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> removeElement(vector<int> nums, int val) {
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < (int)nums.size(); read++) {
        if (nums[read] != val) {
            nums[write] = nums[read];
            write++;
        }
    }
    nums.resize(write);
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## 5. The one to remember

> **Why now.** The plain reader/writer pass writes every survivor back over itself until the first val shows up, and if val never appears it rewrites the whole array with the values already sitting there — n pointless writes on the commonest input. Checking that the pointers have actually parted turns the 'nothing to remove' case into a pure scan and costs one comparison.

Walk the array with a reader and a writer. The reader visits every position; the writer marks where the next survivor belongs. When the reader finds something other than val it goes to the writer's slot and the writer steps forward — so the gap between them is exactly how many copies of val have been passed, and the survivors land in the order they were read. Skip the copy when the two indices coincide, because writing a value onto itself is work with no effect. When the reader runs out, the writer's position is the length of the answer, and the answer is the prefix ending there.

```python
def remove_element(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != val:
            if read != write:
                nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return nums[:write]
```

**O(n) time · O(1) space**
<details>
<summary>The same rung in Java</summary>

```java
public int[] removeElement(int[] nums, int val) {
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < nums.length; read++) {
        if (nums[read] != val) {
            if (read != write) nums[write] = nums[read];
            write++;
        }
    }
    return Arrays.copyOf(nums, write);
}
```

</details>
<details>
<summary>The same rung in C++</summary>

```cpp
vector<int> removeElement(vector<int> nums, int val) {
    int write = 0;
    for (int read = 0; read < (int)nums.size(); read++) {
        if (nums[read] != val) {
            if (read != write) nums[write] = nums[read];
            write++;
        }
    }
    nums.resize(write);
    return nums;
}
```

</details>

## The arc

| # | Approach | Cost | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Delete and shift | O(n^2) time · O(1) space | the baseline — nothing before it |
| 2 | Filter into a copy | O(n) time · O(n) space | Shifting the tail on every match re-copies values that were already in the right place; an array of nothing but val does that n times, which is quadratic work to produce an empty answer. Appending the survivors somewhere else touches each value exactly once. |
| 3 | Count, then compact | O(n) time · O(1) space | The filtered copy is linear but it allocates a second array the size of the input just to hold values that already exist. Counting first gives the length of the answer up front, so the survivors can be packed into the array that was already there and nothing new is allocated. |
| 4 | Reader and writer | O(n) time · O(1) space | The counting pass exists only to learn the length of the answer, and the compaction loop already knows it — the writer's index at the end is that number. Dropping the first pass halves the reads and removes a second place where the match test could be written differently by accident. |
| 5 | The one to remember | O(n) time · O(1) space | The plain reader/writer pass writes every survivor back over itself until the first val shows up, and if val never appears it rewrites the whole array with the values already sitting there — n pointless writes on the commonest input. Checking that the pointers have actually parted turns the 'nothing to remove' case into a pure scan and costs one comparison. |

## Full runnable script

Every rung in one file, printed against the inputs `npm run verify:run`
drives the Java and C++ blocks with. Run it: `python explained.py`.

```python
def remove_element_delete_and_shift(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        if nums[i] == val:
            for j in range(i, n - 1):
                nums[j] = nums[j + 1]
            n -= 1
        else:
            i += 1
    return nums[:n]


def remove_element_filter_into_a_copy(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    kept = []
    for x in nums:
        if x != val:
            kept.append(x)
    return kept


def remove_element_count_then_compact(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    keep = 0
    for x in nums:
        if x != val:
            keep += 1
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != val:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return nums[:keep]


def remove_element_reader_and_writer(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != val:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return nums[:write]


def remove_element_the_one_to_remember(nums: list[int], val: int) -> list[int]:
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != val:
            if read != write:
                nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return nums[:write]

APPROACHES = [
    remove_element_delete_and_shift,
    remove_element_filter_into_a_copy,
    remove_element_count_then_compact,
    remove_element_reader_and_writer,
    remove_element_the_one_to_remember,
]

# the same inputs npm run verify:run drives the Java and C++ blocks with:
# the writer that lags behind the reader — [0,1,2,2,3,0,4,2] has two matches in a row, and [2,2,2] never lets the writer move at all
CASES = [
    lambda: ([3,2,2,3], 3),
    lambda: ([0,1,2,2,3,0,4,2], 2),
    lambda: ([], 0),
    lambda: ([2,2,2], 2),
    lambda: ([1], 2),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for fn in APPROACHES:
        answers = []
        for make in CASES:
            try:
                answers.append(fn(*make()))
            except BaseException as exc:  # a rung that raises names itself
                answers.append(f"!{exc}")
        print(f"{fn.__name__:<36} -> {answers}")
```
